subject: Clarifying dedicated capacity guarantees & queueing behavior
messages:
From: Mira Gomez <mira@clarityai.com>
To: ben_carter@redwood.com
Cc: lauren_bishop@redwood.com
Date: Mon, 4 Aug 2025 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Dedicated capacity — throughput SLAs and queueing question

Hi Ben (and Lauren),

Thanks again for the demo last week. Our infra and procurement teams reviewed the Dedicated offering and have a couple of follow-ups before we move to procurement:

1) When you state a per-tenant throughput guarantee (tokens/sec), is that enforced per reserved GPU or averaged across the dedicated pool? We need to know how steady-state latency behaves under bursty traffic.

2) How does Redwood handle tenant preemption during maintenance or noisy neighbors — are requests queued and rate-limited, or dropped/redirected to a compatible hosted fallback? The difference matters for our SLA with customers.

3) If queueing occurs, what is the max tail latency we should assume for 99.9th percentile for 1–10s request bursts?

I've attached a short spreadsheet with the specific workload patterns (batch sizes, typical seq lengths). Can you loop in anyone from runtime/ops who can confirm behavior?

Appreciate a quick note so we can assess risk for our SRE and procurement reviews.

Best,
Mira Gomez
Head of Platform
ClarityAI

From: ben_carter@redwood.com

Cc: lauren_bishop@redwood.com, karthik_iyer@redwood.com
Date: Mon, 4 Aug 2025 12:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity — throughput SLAs and queueing question

Hi Mira —

Thanks for the clear notes and the spreadsheet. Short answers up front and then I'll loop in Karthik from capacity engineering for the deep details:

- Per-tenant throughput guarantees are expressed at the reserved-capacity level (i.e., the reserved GPU pool we allocate for your account). We guarantee minimum throughput for the pool you reserve; how that maps to individual instances (GPUs) depends on the sizing of the reserved pool.

- During maintenance or noisy-neighbor events we have two mechanisms: (1) preferred behavior is traffic queuing within the pool with backpressure and (2) optional automatic fallback to a hosted-compatible model variant if you enable cross-tier fallback. We can surface both behaviors in the SLA addendum.

- For tail latency: for typical seq lengths matching your spreadsheet (avg ~128 tokens, spikes to 512), our safe planning number for 99.9p tail under steady load is ~400–600ms with a properly sized reserved pool; if you enable fallback the effective 99.9p goes down but adds cross-variant consistency considerations. Karthik will share exact numbers for your requested reserve sizes.

I'll ask Karthik to give a node-level breakdown and propose wording for the SLA carveouts (maintenance window, preemption, fallback).

Best,
Ben Carter
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference

From: karthik_iyer@redwood.com

Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity — throughput SLAs and queueing question

Hi all — looping in with the deeper numbers. I pulled the workload patterns from the spreadsheet and ran them against two representative reserved pool sizes (4x A100-equivalent and 16x A100-equivalent). Summary:

- Guaranteed throughput is expressed as a pool-level token/sec minimum. For 4x the practical steady-state guarantee is ~52k tokens/sec; for 16x it's ~210k tokens/sec. Those are conservative and assume no KV-cache hits and 95th percentile token costs.

- Queueing behavior: we use a latency-first queue that keeps requests in-memory on the pool; requests are not dropped unless the queue exceeds configured max_inflight (default 2048). When the queue hits the soft limit we apply token-level rate limiting (adaptive backpressure) which slows inflight acceptance — so you will see increased queuing but not silent drops.

- Maintenance/preemption: we do rolling maintenance with a cross-pool drain window. If you opt-in to cross-tier fallback we will route affected requests to a compatible hosted model; those requests will be billed at hosted pricing and marked in tracing as fallback. Fallback is opt-in because it changes determinism.

- Tail: With your average profile the empirical 99.9p is ~650ms for the 4x pool during short spikes; for the 16x pool it's ~220–320ms. The 650ms number includes queueing at soft-limit; if you want a hard SLO at 99.9p <500ms we recommend 16x (or 12x with KV-cache warm).

I'm happy to convert these into SLA language (credits, measurement windows). Suggest we add a carveout for scheduled maintenance (we propose a 2-hour monthly window) and an emergency mitigation clause.

Karthik
Sr. Engineering Manager, Capacity

From: lauren_bishop@redwood.com

Date: Thu, 7 Aug 2025 10:12:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity — throughput SLAs and queueing question

Hi Mira — thanks for the clear list. A few operational commitments we can include in the SLA addendum: 

- Credit formula: If the measured monthly pool throughput falls below the guaranteed throughput (measured over a 1-minute sliding window aggregated across the pool), credits will be calculated as (minutes_below_threshold / total_measured_minutes_in_month) * monthly_reserved_fee * credit_multiplier. Standard credit_multiplier: 0.5 for first occurrence, 1.0 for repeated breaches after remediation. We can adapt the multiplier per negotiation.

- Data residency for fallback: confirmed — we will restrict fallback routing to the same geographic region (EU) unless you explicitly opt into cross-region fallback. We'll include a clause enumerating the eligible model variants for fallback.

- max_inflight/backpressure: default 2048 is configurable per contract. Once the hard queue limit is reached new requests receive a 429 with x-retry-after. After a prolonged exceedance (configurable threshold, default 5 minutes) the pool will mark requests as throttled and, if fallback is disabled, will escalate per the incident runbook (alerts and crediting as above). We'll include exact thresholds in the addendum.

Proposal: Ben — can you propose a 30-minute call tomorrow with Mira + SRE + Karthik to finalize the numbers? If we can lock the pool size (e.g., 12x) we'll produce a redline.

Thanks,
Lauren Bishop
Director, Customer Success
